content:
My problem is: If I need to restructure my project (changing file structure architecture and especially moving lemmas around between files, changing import/DAG mapping), I quite often run into a desynch between VS Code and the lake compiler, where my project builds from the shell but VS Code doesn't recognize the new dependency graph, for what I assume to be is a desynch in the olean files. Adding a blank line to a file and saving and resetting the server sometimes resolves the problem, but more often than not, I have to use "lake clean" and then rebuild the project from shell.

I try to regularly update my lake build, and save files even more so, and do any changes incrementally. I always build the new file structures and import dependency paths before adding additional code. This helps, but I just cannot avoid this situation 100%, especially when doing a major restructuring.

My project is at 20,000+ lines of code and contains two libraries currently each with 4 to 5 folders and some of these contain 3 to 5 subfolders ( I won't go deeper per Mathlib standards instructions). It compiles very nicely (thank you, lean4 team!) but restructuring is inevitable as the project develops and a lake clean/lake build takes around 2 to 3 hours, currently.

Is there anything I am doing wrong? Is there anything I am not doing that will help? I am new to lean so there's certainly something I am doing at least somewhat wrong. I've also searched this forum for relevant topics and didn't find anything immediately pertinent, so apologies if I missed it here.. I've also done my best to read and reread the documentation but I get overloaded with information :(

Edit: Im running on windows 10. It's not fun, and I am seriously considering going back to Linux now.

Thank you,
Ian

PostEdit: Another example: I just deleted a file that was unused and turned out I wouldnt need. It had the import pathing implemented however. I deleted it inside of VS code, and edited the barrel file that imported it to remove the import command also inside VS code. And this resulted in compilation errors because VS code did not delete the requisite olean etc files. To resolve the issue, I had to manually delete the related ilean/olean/trace files inside of .lake (so VS code doesnt talk to lake I guess when deleting files) and then (probably a windows problem) I had to delete the workspace for VS code to get it to reboot with clean pathing. And then I had to manually restart every single file (because apparently neither restarting the window nor the server does this) in dependency order... A lot of work for deleting an almost empty file. Still faster than running lake clean/build.

Ian Allen said:

and edited the barrel file

This sounds like you are doing something you should not be doing! Even the word "barrel" is an internal lake implementation detail that no user should have interact with.

umm... I dont know what all the proper nomenclature is so I just use terms that make sense (to me). by "barrel" file, I mean I have a parent folder with a bunch of code.lean files in it, and in the directory containing the parent folder, i have a barrel.lean which simply imports all of the children, nothing else. its not strictly necessary at this point, more for futureproofing, but its the way ive been structuring my file system and dependencies. (I would have loved it however if lean inherited imports... so i could just import my barrel file in later files and get all the children, without having to write up a giant header. that was the original intention, but I couldnt get it to work... its quite possible I am just doing it wrong still learning here.)

either way, with or without a so-called "barrel" file, i still end up having this problematic pattern emerge while editing my project.

It looks like the fastest way to deal with this dependency graph error is

  1. Save all and Git commit the files as is.
  2. Shut down VS code.
  3. delete .lake/build
  4. run lake build (but NOT clean or update)
  5. open VS code and load the project, restarting files in order of dependency.

This will cause lake to iterate through the project very quickly in the areas where there are no changes, and only recompile (or whatever it is doing) in the places where the files have changed. Not sure how it can know what is changed or not when the entire build folder is missing, but it sure seems like this is the behavior..

But I'm going to out on a limb here and guess that maybe the Linux users maybe don't have this kind of problem so often?
